title: Erdős girth conjecture
formal: For every integer \(k\ge 1\), do there exist constants \(c_{k}>0\) and \(N_{k}\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge N_{k}\), some simple undirected graph G on exactly n vertices has at least \(c_{k} n^{1+1/k}\) edges and contains no cycle of length less than \(2k+2\)? Equivalently, is \(M_{2k+2}(n)=\Omega _{k}(n^{1+1/k})\) for every fixed k, where \(M_{s}(n)\) is the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex graph with no cycle shorter than s?
context:
Known extremal upper bounds give \(M_{2k+2}(n)=O_{k}(n^{1+1/k})\). The conjecture asks whether forbidding all these short cycles still permits that many edges up to a constant factor.

Using threshold \(2k+1\) instead of \(2k+2\) gives an equivalent asymptotic conjecture: a graph has a bipartite subgraph with at least half its edges, and that subgraph has no odd cycles. This equivalence changes neither the exponent nor the fixed-k target.

The cases \(k=1,2,3,5\) are known. The July 2026 spanner paper still lists exactly those cases; the next missing parameter \(k=4\) asks for \(\Omega (n^{5/4})\) edges with girth at least 10.

The source uses these graphs to establish conditional lower bounds on the memory needed by routing schemes with small stretch. More generally, the conjecture controls sharpness of size-versus-stretch bounds for graph spanners.

The 2026 preprint removes this assumption for a particular model of spanners tolerating edge failures of bounded degree. It explicitly distinguishes that result from constructing graphs of the girth and density required here.

This additional occurrence comes from the same compact-routing paper. The retained formal statement fixes its own girth threshold and graph-size quantifiers; a differently quantified girth conjecture is not automatically identified with it.
why: A central extremal graph question with direct consequences for compact routing and graph sparsification: it asks whether the standard density obstruction from short cycles is asymptotically tight at every fixed scale.

definitions: A simple undirected graph consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; loops and repeated edges are not allowed. A cycle of length \(\ell\)\(\ge 3\) has \(\ell\) distinct vertices and the edges joining them cyclically. The girth is the length of the shortest cycle, and is +∞ for a forest. Thus “girth at least \(2k+2\)” forbids every cycle of lengths \(3,\ldots ,2k+1\), including non-induced cycles. \(M_{s}(n)\) is a maximum over all such graphs on the vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); connectedness, regularity and efficient construction are not required. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists c_{k},N_{k} \forall n\ge N_{k} \exists G\). Constants may depend on k, but not on n; k remains fixed as n tends to infinity. The target is the stated constant-factor asymptotic density, not merely \(n^{1+1/k- o(1)}\), nor a claim for an arbitrarily sparse subsequence of n. This at-least-girth convention reproduces the source’s definition.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence claim for every fixed integer k, or refute it for at least one fixed k. Refutation means that no positive \(c_{k}\) and threshold \(N_{k}\) work at that k; a construction for only selected k or a smaller exponent does not settle the universal conjecture.
